title: Legal & Ethical — Torts in Depth: Negligence, Malpractice, Assault/Battery & False Imprisonment (Set 7)
subtitle: Torts vs crimes, intentional vs unintentional torts, the elements of negligence/malpractice (duty, breach, causation, damages), malpractice as professional negligence, assault vs battery, false imprisonment (including improper restraint), defamation (libel/slander), invasion of privacy, consent, liability, and prevention through standards and documentation
scenario: Understanding the civil wrongs (torts) most relevant to psychiatric-technician practice—how negligence and malpractice are judged, the difference between assault and battery, what constitutes false imprisonment, and how following standards and documenting well reduce legal risk.

steps.q: A tort is best described as:

opts.text: A civil wrong that causes harm to another person, for which the injured party may seek damages
opts.rat: Torts are civil wrongs; the harmed person may sue for compensation, in contrast to crimes, which are offenses against the state.

opts.text: A crime punishable only by imprisonment
opts.rat: That describes criminal law; torts are civil wrongs handled through civil claims.

opts.text: A type of medical treatment
opts.rat: A tort is a legal concept, not a treatment.

opts.text: A facility policy
opts.rat: A tort is a civil wrong recognized by law, not an internal policy.

steps.q: Torts are commonly divided into:

opts.text: Intentional torts and unintentional torts (such as negligence)
opts.rat: Intentional torts involve a deliberate act (e.g., battery), while unintentional torts—chiefly negligence—involve a failure to act with reasonable care.

opts.text: Only crimes and misdemeanors
opts.rat: Those are criminal-law terms, not the tort categories.

opts.text: Federal and state taxes
opts.rat: Taxes are unrelated to tort categories.

opts.text: Written and verbal contracts
opts.rat: Contracts are a separate area of law, not the categories of torts.

steps.q: Negligence is best described as:

opts.text: Failing to act as a reasonably careful person would in a similar situation, resulting in harm
opts.rat: Negligence is a failure to meet the standard of reasonable care that a prudent person would use, leading to harm.

opts.text: A deliberate plan to injure someone
opts.rat: A deliberate act to injure would be an intentional tort, not negligence.

opts.text: Always a criminal act with no civil aspect
opts.rat: Negligence is generally a civil (tort) matter, though outcomes can be serious.

opts.text: Doing everything correctly and carefully
opts.rat: That is the opposite of negligence.

steps.q: To prove negligence or malpractice, generally all of these elements must be shown:

opts.text: A duty to the client, a breach of that duty, that the breach caused harm, and actual damages
opts.rat: The classic elements are duty, breach (dereliction) of duty, causation (the breach caused the harm), and damages.

opts.text: Only that the client was unhappy with care
opts.rat: Dissatisfaction alone does not establish negligence; all elements must be present.

opts.text: Only that a bad outcome occurred
opts.rat: A bad outcome without a breach that caused it does not establish negligence.

opts.text: Only that the staff member was tired
opts.rat: Fatigue alone is not one of the required elements.

steps.q: How does malpractice relate to negligence?

opts.text: Malpractice is professional negligence—a licensed professional's failure to meet the standard of care
opts.rat: Malpractice is negligence committed by a professional acting in their professional role, judged against the professional standard of care.

opts.text: Malpractice has nothing to do with negligence
opts.rat: Malpractice is a specific form of negligence by a professional.

opts.text: Malpractice applies only to non-professionals
opts.rat: Malpractice specifically involves professionals.

opts.text: Malpractice means always providing excellent care
opts.rat: Malpractice refers to substandard professional care, not excellent care.

steps.q: When judging whether a technician was negligent, their actions are compared to:

opts.text: What a reasonably prudent technician with similar training would have done in the same situation
opts.rat: The standard of care is what a reasonably prudent, similarly trained person would do under like circumstances.

opts.text: What the most expensive specialist in the world would do
opts.rat: The comparison is to a reasonably prudent peer, not an extraordinary specialist.

opts.text: Whatever the technician personally felt like doing
opts.rat: Personal preference is not the legal standard.

opts.text: What produces the fastest results regardless of safety
opts.rat: Speed over safety is not the standard of care.

steps.q: Assault, as an intentional tort, is best described as:

opts.text: An act that makes a person reasonably fear imminent harmful or offensive contact—no actual touching is required
opts.rat: Assault is creating a reasonable apprehension of imminent harmful or offensive contact; the threat itself, without touching, can constitute assault.

opts.text: Only physically striking a person
opts.rat: Physical contact is battery; assault is the threat that creates fear of contact.

opts.text: Writing a false statement about someone
opts.rat: That describes defamation (libel), not assault.

opts.text: Confining someone against their will
opts.rat: That describes false imprisonment, not assault.

steps.q: Battery, as an intentional tort, is best described as:

opts.text: Actual harmful or offensive physical contact with a person without their consent
opts.rat: Battery is the unconsented harmful or offensive touching of another person.

opts.text: Only threatening a person with words
opts.rat: A threat without contact is assault; battery requires actual contact.

opts.text: Spreading a rumor about a person
opts.rat: That is defamation (slander), not battery.

opts.text: Locking a person in a room
opts.rat: That is false imprisonment, not battery.

steps.q: A technician tells a client, 'If you don't hold still, I'll give you this injection whether you like it or not,' and then injects the client who has refused. Which torts are illustrated?

opts.text: The threat is assault and the unconsented injection is battery
opts.rat: The threat creating fear of imminent contact is assault; carrying out the unconsented contact is battery.

opts.text: Only defamation
opts.rat: Defamation involves false statements harming reputation, which is not what occurred here.

opts.text: Only false imprisonment
opts.rat: The scenario centers on a threat and unconsented contact—assault and battery.

opts.text: No tort at all
opts.rat: A threat plus unconsented contact clearly involves assault and battery.

steps.q: False imprisonment is best described as:

opts.text: Unlawfully restricting a person's freedom of movement without proper justification or consent
opts.rat: False imprisonment is confining or restraining a person's movement without legal justification or consent.

opts.text: Making a person afraid of being touched
opts.rat: That describes assault, not false imprisonment.

opts.text: Touching a person without consent
opts.rat: That describes battery, not false imprisonment.

opts.text: Writing something false about a person
opts.rat: That describes defamation, not false imprisonment.

steps.q: Which situation could constitute false imprisonment?

opts.text: Restraining or secluding a client without proper justification or order, or refusing to let a voluntary client leave
opts.rat: Improper restraint/seclusion and preventing a voluntary client from leaving without legal grounds can be false imprisonment.

opts.text: Applying a properly ordered, justified restraint to prevent imminent harm
opts.rat: A properly justified, ordered intervention to prevent harm is not false imprisonment.

opts.text: Encouraging a client to attend a voluntary group
opts.rat: Encouragement is not confinement.

opts.text: Reminding a client of unit rules
opts.rat: Reminding a client of rules does not restrict their freedom unlawfully.

steps.q: Defamation involves:

opts.text: Making a false statement that harms another person's reputation—libel if written, slander if spoken
opts.rat: Defamation is a false statement that damages reputation; written defamation is libel and spoken defamation is slander.

opts.text: Any true statement about a client
opts.rat: Truth is generally a defense; defamation involves false statements.

opts.text: Touching a client without consent
opts.rat: That is battery, not defamation.

opts.text: Confining a client to a room
opts.rat: That is false imprisonment, not defamation.

steps.q: Sharing or exposing a client's private information or body without authorization can constitute:

opts.text: Invasion of privacy
opts.rat: Unauthorized disclosure or exposure of a client's private information or person can be the tort of invasion of privacy.

opts.text: Negligence in medication administration
opts.rat: That describes a different kind of error, not invasion of privacy.

opts.text: A properly authorized disclosure
opts.rat: Authorized disclosures are lawful; invasion of privacy is unauthorized.

opts.text: A standard part of care
opts.rat: Unauthorized exposure of private information is not a standard, acceptable practice.

steps.q: Providing treatment or contact to a client who has validly refused it can result in:

opts.text: A claim of battery, because the contact was without consent
opts.rat: Unconsented treatment or touching—especially after a valid refusal—can constitute battery.

opts.text: No legal concern whatsoever
opts.rat: Unconsented contact can be battery; consent and refusal must be respected.

opts.text: Automatic praise for being thorough
opts.rat: Overriding a valid refusal is a legal risk, not praiseworthy.

opts.text: A defamation claim
opts.rat: Defamation involves false statements, not unconsented contact.

steps.q: A common way to reduce the risk of negligence/malpractice claims is to:

opts.text: Follow standards of care, policies, and one's scope of practice, and communicate and document accurately
opts.rat: Adhering to standards, staying within scope, and clear, accurate documentation and communication both improve care and reduce legal risk.

opts.text: Take shortcuts to work faster
opts.rat: Shortcuts that deviate from the standard increase risk of harm and liability.

opts.text: Work outside one's scope to be helpful
opts.rat: Acting outside scope increases both client risk and legal exposure.

opts.text: Avoid documenting to save time
opts.rat: Poor documentation increases risk; accurate records are protective.

steps.q: How does accurate documentation help protect against liability?

opts.text: It provides an accurate record showing what care was given and that the standard of care was met
opts.rat: Timely, factual documentation demonstrates the care provided and supports that appropriate care was delivered.

opts.text: It guarantees no one can ever file a claim
opts.rat: Documentation does not prevent all claims, but it supports the defense that proper care was given.

opts.text: It matters only if the outcome was bad
opts.rat: Accurate documentation is important for all care, not only bad outcomes.

opts.text: It allows staff to alter records after the fact
opts.rat: Altering records is itself improper and increases liability.

steps.q: Regarding liability, generally:

opts.text: The person who commits the tort is responsible, and the facility may also share liability
opts.rat: Individuals are accountable for their own actions, and employers/facilities may share liability for acts within employment.

opts.text: Only the facility is ever responsible, never the individual
opts.rat: Individuals remain accountable for their own conduct.

opts.text: No one is responsible for a tort
opts.rat: Torts create responsibility for the resulting harm.

opts.text: Only the client is responsible
opts.rat: The client is the harmed party, not the responsible party for the staff's tort.

steps.q: Which is an example of an UNINTENTIONAL tort?

opts.text: A client is harmed because the technician carelessly failed to follow a basic safety standard
opts.rat: Careless failure to meet a standard causing harm is negligence—an unintentional tort.

opts.text: Deliberately striking a client in anger
opts.rat: A deliberate harmful act is an intentional tort (battery).

opts.text: Purposely locking a client in a room without justification
opts.rat: Intentional unjustified confinement is an intentional tort (false imprisonment).

opts.text: Knowingly spreading a false, damaging rumor
opts.rat: Deliberate false statements harming reputation is an intentional tort (defamation).

steps.q: If the technician makes an error that could harm a client, the appropriate response is to:

opts.text: Report it honestly and promptly per policy so the client can be protected and cared for
opts.rat: Prompt, honest reporting allows the team to protect the client and is both ethical and part of risk management.

opts.text: Hide the error to avoid getting in trouble
opts.rat: Concealing an error endangers the client and increases liability.

opts.text: Alter the record to cover it up
opts.rat: Falsifying records is a serious violation that compounds harm and liability.

opts.text: Blame the client for the error
opts.rat: Shifting blame is dishonest and does not protect the client.

steps.q: Match the action to the tort: forcibly keeping a competent voluntary client from leaving the unit without legal grounds is:

opts.text: False imprisonment
opts.rat: Unlawfully preventing a person's free movement without justification is false imprisonment.

opts.text: Defamation
opts.rat: Defamation involves false statements, not restricting movement.

opts.text: Negligence
opts.rat: This is an intentional restriction of freedom, not a careless failure of care.

opts.text: Invasion of privacy
opts.rat: Invasion of privacy involves private information/exposure, not confinement.

reference: Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: Legal & Ethical (LPS Act & Patient Rights) — civil liability/torts. Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references at an introductory level. Concepts are stated conceptually and marked for faculty confirmation: tort vs crime; intentional vs unintentional torts; negligence and its elements (duty, breach, causation, damages); malpractice as professional negligence measured against the standard of care; assault (threat creating fear of contact) vs battery (unconsented contact); false imprisonment (including improper restraint/seclusion or preventing a voluntary client from leaving); defamation (libel/slander); invasion of privacy; the role of consent; shared individual/facility liability; and prevention through standards, scope, communication, and accurate documentation. No specific statutes, code sections, damage amounts, or timeframes are asserted. Extends the malpractice item in legal-core-02, the standard-of-care and record-falsification items in legal-core-04, and connects to restraint law in legal-core-06. Pending faculty review.
